svg.title: RPA's control plane: build in Studio, govern in the Orchestrator, run on Robots
svg.desc: Robotic process automation has three parts. You build workflows in a Studio or IDE, publish them to the Orchestrator, and Robots execute them. The Orchestrator is the control plane: it schedules runs, hands out work from queues, stores credentials and assets centrally so bots never hard-code passwords, and collects logs and analytics. Robots come in two modes. An attended bot runs on a person's desktop, is triggered by that human, shares the machine, and assists front-office work, so it can't run while the user is away. An unattended bot runs headless on a dedicated VM, is scheduled or queue-driven with no human, and handles back-office work at scale. A band explains that RPA drives the user interface of existing apps like a human by clicking, typing, and reading the screen, which needs no backend change and suits legacy systems with no API, but is brittle when the UI changes, so a real API or database integration is preferable when one exists.
svg.text: Build it in Studio, govern it in the Orchestrator, run it on Robots
Studio / IDE
build the workflow
publish
Orchestrator — the control plane
schedule · work queues · credentials/assets · monitoring
assign
Robots
execute the steps
Attended bot
Runs on a person's desktop, triggered by the human,
shares the machine. Front-office assist (e.g. a
call-center helper). Can't run while the user is away.
Unattended bot
Runs headless on a dedicated VM, scheduled or
queue-driven, no human. Back-office work at scale
(overnight batches). The Orchestrator feeds it work.
What a bot actually does: it drives the UI like a human
Clicks, types, and reads the screen of existing apps — no backend change, which is why RPA is the go-to
for legacy systems with no API. The catch: it's brittle — a UI redesign breaks the bot overnight.
The Orchestrator is what makes RPA enterprise-grade rather than a pile of desktop scripts: it schedules runs,
distributes work from queues across a robot fleet, stores credentials centrally (bots never hard-code passwords),
and collects logs and analytics for audit. Design rule: prefer a real API or database integration when one exists —
it's stable and fast. Reach for UI-driving RPA as the glue for systems that expose no other way in.
